stimulus.text:
J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer, Letter III, “What Is an American?”, 1782:

“What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations. He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. ... Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world. ... The American is a new man, who acts upon new principles; he must therefore entertain new ideas, and form new opinions.”
stimulus.source_note: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

primary_sources: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III

stem: In the passage, the phrase “melted into a new race of men” most directly means that...

options.text: people from many nations blended into one American people.
Americans forgot all the languages their parents had spoken.
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about forgetting languages.

options.text: the colonies kept each European nationality separate and distinct.
options.misconception: The passage says the nations are melted into one race, not kept separate.

options.text: Native Americans and Europeans had merged into a single people by 1782.
options.misconception: Background: Crèvecœur writes about Europeans and their descendants; his “new race” leaves Native Americans and enslaved Africans out of the picture.

rationales.A: The passage gives a family of English, Dutch, and French ancestors and says the nations are melted into one people.
rationales.B: The passage never mentions language, so forgetting languages cannot be its meaning.
rationales.C: Melting means blending together, which is the opposite of keeping nationalities separate.
rationales.D: The passage is about Europeans and their descendants, not about a merger with Native Americans.
rationales.general:
1. The passage asks what the American is and answers with a family of mixed European ancestors.
2. It then says individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men.
3. Background: Crèvecœur was a French immigrant writing for European readers in 1782.
4. So “melted” means many nations blended into one American people.
Remember: a metaphor in a source usually points to the idea the writer states just before or after it.
